newsitem.title: SPAIN: Three suitors pursue new Spain telecom Retevision.
newsitem.headline: Three suitors pursue new Spain telecom Retevision.

text.p: Three suitors said on Monday they would like to buy 60 percent of Spain's Retevision, which will face off against market giant Telefonica when it becomes Spain's second basic telephone operator by year end.
Italian public holding STET led off the string of announcements, saying it and Spanish electricity groups Endesa and Union Fenosa, and Basque group Euskatel were interested in Retevision.
They were followed by a widely expected bid from a consortium led by Spain's BCH bank which also groups France Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and U.S. Sprint .
Retevision said that Germany's Mannesmann AG, the second mobile phone operator in Germany, also wants to make an offer -- a surprise entry for many in the market.
Mannesmann was not immediately available to comment.

Monday was the deadline for expressing interest in the group, which has the tough task of competing with Telefonica, which is coming off a triumphant privatisation and last week's announcement of a key new alliance with U.S. based MCI and British Telecommunications .
The period for presentation of bids ends on June 9, and the auction will be resolved in 60 days, but analysts are betting the winner will be BCH if it is prepared to pay a good price.
"The groups' real interest will be reflected in the price," a foreign firm analyst said.
In mid-March, Retevision's board approved the conditions for the sale of a 60 percent stake in the firm for a minimum price of 45.6 billion pesetas ($316.9 million).
The bidder will be obliged to underwrite a 10 percent capital increase in the firm, with a further payment of at least 25.3 billion pesetas.
But aside from the money, analysts said BCH had an edge.
"If I were to bet, I'd bet for the consortium led by BCH," a Madrid-based foreign trading company's analyst said.
Another analyst said that BCH, whose group made its interest public weeks ago, appeared more thought out in its approach.
"The BCH group seems more stable, the other is giving the impression of being a last-minute alliance," an analyst said.
Another pointed to BCH's telecommunications partners.
"BCH has partners which are strong in technology. STET does not have much experience in international business," an analyst said.
The BCH club's sole problem seems to be a reduced cable network compared with competitors, industry analysts said.
In the STET consortium, Endesa and Union Fenosa will contribute 10,000 km of fibre optic networks for immediate use as an alternative telecoms network to Telefonica.
To help compensate, the BCH group announced on Monday a deal with Spanish railways Renfe which opens the door to using its fibre optic network to strengthen the consortium's bid.

Nevertheless, the government might be worried about failing to award Retevision to Endesa, which it is planning to further privatise in the autumn, and could wish to avoid harming the energy firm's image.
"If Endesa should gain control of Retevision, that will further boost its privatisation this fall," said an analyst.
Analysts added that the forthcoming winner of the auction will be a natural ally of Airtel, Telefonica 's competitor in the mobile telephone sector.

"It would be logical that the second telephone operator in basic phones looks for a deal with the second mobile phone operator," said a source close to one of the two bidders. ($ = 143.8 Spanish Pesetas)
